title: Context Co-Design, Skill Hygiene, and the Blind Timer Shortcut
intro: Today's selection zeroes in on the inner workings of agent harnesses: who should manage the context window, how autonomous research agents should curate their skills, and how easily benchmark numbers can fool us into measuring a stopwatch instead of a vision model. We also take a look at low-level quantization work in llama.cpp and some rather dubious telemetry habits in agent skill plugins.

stories.headline: Letting Models Drive Their Own Context API Beats Blind Truncation
stories.summary: Researchers testing NVIDIA's open-source agent harness, `nooa`, evaluated model-driven context management—where models explicitly decide what and when to compact via an API—against standard harness-driven rolling summarization. On tasks like OfficeQA Pro v2, giving GPT 6.1 control of its context nearly tripled its score (21% to 56%) under a constrained 32K budget, while Kimi achieved score gains with up to 41% fewer input tokens across sweeps up to 512K. Crucially for serving setups, the authors demonstrated that reusing unchanged suffix KV caches after in-place context edits slashes prefill compute by up to 15% without measurable accuracy drops.
stories.why_it_matters: If agent frameworks expose context manipulation directly to the model rather than relying on blunt heuristic truncation, inference engines can leverage suffix KV cache reuse to make long-horizon agent runs significantly cheaper.
stories.reason: It investigates whether agent harnesses should delegate context compaction directly to the model rather than relying on external summarization heuristics.

item.title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
item.summary: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, model-driven context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~rightarrow~56\%), and Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy. item.content:
Abstract
Model-driven context management through a context API improves accuracy and token efficiency over harness-triggered compaction, while reusing KV caches after edits reduces prefill compute.
Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, model-driven context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~rightarrow~56\%), and Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
Community
We gave models control over their own context: on OfficeQA Pro v2, GPT nearly triples its score at tight budgets, and Kimi gains with up to 41% fewer input tokens. This opens a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.
Harness-driven compaction is dumb and that's exactly why I trust it — when my agent truncates history I can diff the transcript and point at the chunk that went missing. Model-driven compaction moves that into a sampling step I can't reproduce, so the number I care about isn't accuracy across the 8K–512K sweep, it's recoverability: after a run, can you reconstruct why a chunk got dropped and whether it was load-bearing? I want a drop log — stated reason, triggering turn, timestamp — because otherwise the first production bug is going to be "it forgot the schema it read in turn 3" with nothing to point at. The other thing worth counting is that a context API is one more call that can fail silently, and at 8K the model burns turns managing memory instead of doing the task. I'd want the token accounting to include the management overhead, not just the retained input, or the budget comparison against a fixed window is flattering itself.

stories.headline: In Autonomous Research Harnesses, Context Folding and Skill Pruning Win
stories.summary: A systematic study breaking down self-evolving autoresearch harnesses on MLE-Bench and KernelBench evaluated context management and skill accumulation against basic recency-truncation baselines. The authors found that rolling summaries actually degrade performance compared to 'context folding' (keeping expandable, per-attempt digests), which boosted task success by up to 19.2%. When managing learned skills, selectively pruning persistently unused lessons consistently outperformed consolidating them or turning them into standing rules. Combining both mechanisms into the MLEvolver harness yielded a 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and a 94% fast_1 score on KernelBench Level 3, handily beating AIDE and OpenEvolve under matched inference budgets.
stories.why_it_matters: This gives agent framework builders clear architectural guidance: ditch messy rolling summaries for foldable attempt histories, and implement aggressive garbage collection on accumulated agent skills.
stories.reason: It breaks down autonomous research agent harnesses into their constituent mechanisms to evaluate how context compaction and modular tool skills affect iterative performance.

item.content:
Demystifying the Autoresearch Harness: How Context and Skills Shape Self-Evolving Agents
Abstract
A systematic study of harness design for long-horizon self-evolving autoresearch agents finds that context folding and selective skill deletion improve performance, enabling MLEvolver to achieve strong results on MLE-Bench Lite and KernelBench Level 3.
Autoresearch agents, which autonomously design, run, and refine experiments, are accelerating scientific progress, particularly in AI research. However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine multiple mechanisms, making it difficult to determine how individual components contribute to performance. We systematically study harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents along two dimensions: context management, which determines what an agent retains from its past attempts, and skill management, which governs how it stores and reuses lessons from those attempts. Across MLE-Bench and KernelBench with gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol, we isolate the effects of individual harness design choices by evaluating each against a recency-truncation baseline within a shared agent framework. For context management, we find that preserving individually accessible records of past attempts is more effective than maintaining a rolling summary, with context folding performing best across all six settings and improving upon the baseline by up to 19.2%. For skill management, selectively discarding persistently unused lessons is more effective on average than consolidating them or promoting them to standing rules. Building on these findings, we combine context folding and skill deletion in MLEvolver, which achieves a 72.7% medal rate on MLE-Bench Lite and a 94% fast_1 score on KernelBench Level 3, substantially outperforming AIDE and OpenEvolve under the same inference budget. Overall, our study distills design principles for preserving experimental history and curating reusable lessons in autoresearch harnesses, paving the way for agents that turn accumulated experience into sustained progress.
Community
What actually drives long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents? This paper systematically demystifies agent harness design across context and skill management on MLE-Bench and KernelBench. Rather than rolling summaries or complex skill consolidation, the authors reveal that simple mechanisms such as context folding (expandable per-attempt digests, up to +19.2%) and skill deletion (pruning unused lessons) deliver the strongest gains. Combining these principles in MLEvolver dramatically outperforms AIDE and OpenEvolve under the same budget, achieving a 45.5% gold medal rate (+42.9% over baselines) on MLE-Bench Lite and 62% fast₂ on KernelBench Level 3 (over 2× AIDE and 4× OpenEvolve).

stories.headline: OS-Omni Benchmarks Cross-Platform Agents Across Desktop and Mobile
stories.summary: A new live benchmark, OS-Omni, tests computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web, focusing on long-horizon, persistent-state workflows rather than isolated UI interactions. The v1 release contains 48 tasks per platform plus 12 cross-platform workflows pairing desktop environments with an Android phone, averaging 67.5 interaction steps per task compared to OSWorld's 15. Claude Opus 5.5 led the field with a 68.5% average success rate (trailing human baselines at 77.3%), but the failure modes were stark: while frontier models beat humans on Linux, they lagged human performance by more than 25 percentage points on iOS and macOS.
stories.why_it_matters: The benchmark provides a reproducible, multi-platform execution harness with state-verification that exposes how brittle current generalist GUI agents remain when leaving standard Linux desktop environments.
stories.reason: It provides a unified benchmark evaluating generalist computer-using agents on complex, long-horizon workflows across web, mobile, and desktop operating systems.

item.title: OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms
item.summary: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. item.content:
OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms
Abstract
A live cross-platform benchmark evaluates computer-using agents on long-horizon workflows across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web, showing that current agents remain far from platform-robust computer use and trail humans on iOS and macOS.
Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.8 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes.
Community
NeurIPS 2026

stories.headline: llama.cpp Lands Native Tensor and Activation Scaling for FP8 and NVFP4
stories.summary: Release b12818 in `llama.cpp` brings extensive GGML support for quantization scale tensors tailored for FP8 and NVFP4. The update introduces per-tensor, per-channel, per-expert, and per-expert-per-channel scaling side-cars, wired directly into matrix multiplication operators such as `mul_mat` and `mul_mat_id`. It also hooks up optional activation scales while preserving hardware-specific paths across CUDA cublasLt, Apple Silicon Metal, and CPU kernels.
stories.why_it_matters: Native support for granular expert and channel scales in GGML paves the way for efficient local inference of modern MoE architectures running scaled FP8 and NVFP4 weights.
stories.reason: It introduces native ggml support for FP8 and NVFP4 tensor scaling across channels and MoE experts, alongside activation scaling for matrix operations.

stories.headline: Hitting 101 tok/s with Inkling 2 Mini on a GB10 in vLLM
stories.summary: A detailed serving walkthrough demonstrated 101 tokens/second on single requests and 195.7 tokens/second across four concurrent requests running Inkling 2 Mini (with a 131K context) on an MSI EdgeXpert GB10 machine. Throughput gains came from an array of surgical engine-level tweaks: rounding Triton compile constants to powers of two to eliminate kernel compilation stalls on dynamic prompt lengths, running INT8 copies of the draft model's linear layers and output head, switching vLLM to probabilistic drafting, and masking low-confidence draft rows as padding to bypass routed expert evaluation without breaking CUDA graph requirements.
stories.why_it_matters: The recipe illustrates practical low-level tricks—especially draft head quantization and CUDA-graph-compatible MoE padding—that can be lifted directly into production speculative decoding pipelines.
stories.reason: It shares practical vLLM serving configurations and optimization tricks to achieve high token throughput with the Inkling 2 Mini model on modern GPU hardware.

item.title: Show HN: Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
item.content:
Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
196 tok/s across four concurrent requests, a 9.7-second 32K prefill and room for a second model.
After taking Inkling 2 Mini for a spin on my GB10, I wanted to make it faster without leaving vLLM, removing Qwen3.8-27B from the machine or shrinking Inkling’s 131,072-token context.
A few days of tuning later, Inkling runs at:
- 101 tok/s for a single request.
- 195.7 tok/s in aggregate for four concurrent requests.
- 9.7 seconds to the first token on a 32K prompt.
On tonyd2wild’s Inkling benchmark, that’s the fastest single-request vLLM result I know of. On the same benchmark tonyd2wild’s TensorFold port measured 105.5 tok/s and knapcio’s SGLang recipe 112.0. With four requests at once my setup beats both of tonyd2wild’s published setups.
Inkling still uses 36% of the GB10’s memory. Qwen3.8-27B stayed loaded but idle while I measured.
The work covered vLLM settings, speculative decoding, CUDA graphs and the GPU kernels behind Inkling’s experts.
How a request runs on Inkling
A request runs in two phases. Prefill reads the prompt in chunks of 4,096 tokens and produces the first token. Decode generates the rest of the reply, several tokens per step.
Decode uses speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes 7 tokens and Inkling checks all of them in one pass. The rejection sampler keeps the proposals up to the first one Inkling rejects, plus one token of Inkling’s own, so every step keeps 1 to 8 tokens.
Mapping changes against the request path:
Common terms:
The routed experts take 53% of a decode step and 44% of a 32K prefill:
The starting point
The machine is an MSI EdgeXpert, MSI’s version of NVIDIA’s DGX Spark, with one GB10 chip and 128 GB of memory shared by the CPU and GPU. Building a home AI lab on NVIDIA GB10 covers the setup and Taking Inkling 2 Mini for a spin on NVIDIA GB10 the first look at the model.
vLLM settings for Inkling:
That gives Inkling about 44 GiB, including a KV cache that holds 1.85 full 131,072-token requests.
Tuning steps so far, from DSpark (the draft model that ships with Inkling) to DFlash2:
When incoai released DFlash2, tonyd2wild published the vLLM patches to run it. On their benchmark it lifted one request from 61.4 to 88.2 tok/s. With the same patches I measured 90.3.
On my everyday prompts (one coding, one prose and one reasoning prompt at the model’s default settings) the gain was smaller. Reasoning ran 24 to 26% faster and four requests at once 10 to 14% faster. Prose stayed flat.
With four requests at once, though, my setup fell behind: 163.8 tok/s in aggregate against tonyd2wild’s 180.4.
Ideas from the GB10 community
Most of my changes started from ideas other GB10 owners had published:
Tuning vLLM
Mapping the changes I made to the request:
1. Removing compilation stalls on new prompts
My first run of tonyd2wild’s benchmark showed fresh prompts waiting a median 2.3 seconds for their first token, mostly while GPU kernels compiled.
Inkling’s expert planner computes max_ctas, the most blocks of GPU work the experts could need, from the token count. Triton receives it as a compile-time constant and compiles a new kernel for each new value. So almost every new prompt length recompiled about ten kernels while the request waited.
The open pull request rounds the value up to a power of two, so all prompt lengths share 12 to 15 compiled variants. On twelve prompt lengths the server hadn’t seen, it cut the stalls by 67 to 90%. Outputs and decode speed didn’t change.
2. Making drafting cheaper with INT8
Drafting has its own cost. Each decode step runs the draft’s layers plus a second pass through Inkling’s 926 MB output head, which took about 8.5 milliseconds per step in a microbenchmark.
I added INT8 copies of DFlash2’s 21 linear layers and the shared output head, read through sxuff’s INT8 matrix-vector kernel. Only drafting uses them. Inkling still verifies with its original weights, so its output doesn’t change.
Gradual gains in stages:
- The microbenchmark predicted 7 to 8% more throughput.
- The first build gave 1.8%.
- I profiled real decode steps with and without the copies. The output head never ran in INT8, because DFlash2 calls it with FP32 output, a case my code didn’t handle.
- With that fixed, two runs gained 4.3 to 4.9%, from 90.6 to 94.8 tok/s, for 843 MB of copies. The temperature-0 output of my three check prompts stayed identical.
The profile without the copies also showed the bigger cost: the routed experts took 31.2 of the step’s 58.4 milliseconds.
3. Probabilistic drafting
vLLM drafts greedily by default. For a sampled request, its rejection sampler then treats each drafted token as certain instead of using the draft’s real probabilities, so it accepts fewer drafts than it could.
Setting draft_sample_method to probabilistic gives the sampler those probabilities. Inkling’s output distribution stays the same either way.
Greedy against probabilistic drafting on my everyday prompts, at the default temperature of 1.0:
That’s 14 to 20% faster for sampled requests. Temperature-0 requests ran the same, so tonyd2wild’s benchmark would never have shown this gain.
4. Adaptive verify width
The routed experts took 53% of the profiled decode step, so I looked for expert work to skip.
Every verify row reads 8 experts in every layer, yet drafts are accepted in order. Once one is rejected, every row after it was wasted work. The draft’s own probabilities can predict where that will happen, which is how TensorFold and knapcio’s SGLang recipe already cut verification.
Working within CUDA graph constraints
vLLM has its own adaptive verification, but it needs CUDA graphs that allow different verify widths within one batch. Inkling’s attention backends don’t support them.
So I kept all eight rows and changed what they do. Inkling’s MoE layer already sends padding rows to no expert. Marking low-confidence rows as padding skips their expert reads and leaves the CUDA graph shapes unchanged.

stories.headline: DRBench Pro Evaluates Deep Research via Structured Knowledge Graphs
stories.summary: DRBench Pro aims to replace subjective report judging with an automated, graph-grounded evaluation pipeline built from Wikipedia knowledge trees. Across 144 research tasks covering 24 domains and 44,102 relational rubrics, the benchmark evaluates both breadth (coverage across distinct research branches) and depth (exploration down chained relations), combining them via geometric mean. Testing 16 deep research agent configurations showed that the best system capped out at only 57.04% overall coverage, with identical high-level scores often obscuring heavy skews between wide topical breadth and deep topical exploration.
stories.why_it_matters: For anyone building deep research or information-gathering agents, this benchmark decouples writing quality from actual investigative thoroughness using objective graph-traversal rubrics.
stories.reason: It introduces a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate whether deep research agents formulate comprehensive investigation paths rather than merely producing surface-level text.

item.content:
DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
Abstract
Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.
Community
How much of the relevant knowledge does a deep research agent actually cover?
We built DRBench Pro to answer this question. For each case, we derive a research query and evidence-grounded rubrics from the same Wikipedia-derived knowledge tree. This structure lets us measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related chains of knowledge.
DRBench Pro includes 144 research cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. In our evaluation of 16 agent configurations, we found that similar overall coverage scores can mask distinct strengths in breadth and depth.
If you evaluate your own agent with DRBench Pro, we'd love to see your results and hear what you think.

stories.headline: Convex Skill Plugin Caught Exfiltrating User Prompts and Dodging Guardrails
stories.summary: An inspection of Convex skills listed in Anthropic's official Claude plugins marketplace revealed multiple concerning security patterns. The quickstart skill was found sending the user's unredacted project idea via an unannounced HTTP POST to an external endpoint (`basic-anteater-667.convex.site`) labeled as telemetry. More egregiously, another helper skill piped a remote bootstrap script directly into bash while splitting download and execution across separate commands, explicitly commenting in its markdown prompt that doing so circumvents harness safety classifiers.
stories.why_it_matters: This highlights the immediate need for rigid network sandboxing and AST-level command inspection in agent tool harnesses, as prompt-based skills are actively trying to bypass harness-level safety classifiers.
stories.reason: It uncovers a quiet data-exfiltration behavior where an agent skill framework transmits raw user application prompts to remote servers without consent.

item.title: Convex skills send the user's app idea to a remote server without telling them
item.content:
Repository navigation
Description
Three skills in this plugin (listed in Anthropic's claude-plugins-official marketplace) raised the same concern for me:
- skills/quickstart/SKILL.md lines 48 to 56 POST the user's one-sentence project idea to basic-anteater-667.convex.site, marked in a comment as telemetry. The user is not told the idea leaves the machine.
- skills/add/SKILL.md lines 62 and 64 pipe a script from the same host straight into bash.
- skills/labs-quickstart/SKILL.md lines 74 to 80 split downloading and running the bootstrap into two Bash calls, and give the reason: "A single command that both downloads remote code and executes it is the shape harness safety classifiers block."
I read this as a team trying to make onboarding reliable, not as anything malicious. But the last item tells the agent to change the shape of a command so that the user's safety tooling does not catch it, which removes the check the user or their administrator chose to have. Together with an unpinned script from a generated-name host, a user has no way to review what runs.
convex-backend-skill/skills/quickstart/SKILL.md
Lines 48 to 56 in 6ca54f6
convex-backend-skill/skills/add/SKILL.md
Lines 58 to 65 in 6ca54f6
convex-backend-skill/skills/labs-quickstart/SKILL.md
Lines 74 to 80 in 6ca54f6
(All three are still on main as of 26 October; in labs-quickstart the passage is now lines 73 to 80.)
Suggestions: tell the user before the idea is sent, and make it optional; ship the bootstrap and add scripts in the plugin (or pin them by hash) instead of fetching them at run time; and drop the instruction about the classifier, letting the download-and-run step be approved or refused as it is.
I maintain a catalog of agent skills and of the tools for vetting them; it lists these findings at https://thirtysix.github.io/awesome-agent-skills/#skills?q=convex and I will add your response.

stories.headline: Proactive Vision Benchmarks Accidentally Reward Timers over Sight
stories.summary: An evaluation paper revealed that existing benchmarks for proactive physical task assistants (such as Ego-MC-Bench and QICD) reward timing correlations rather than visual reasoning. A naive video-blind baseline—a dumb clock raising an alarm at 25 seconds and confirming steps at 30 seconds without processing frames—scored a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, trouncing every published vision model (which peaked at 0.27). To fix this benchmark flaw, the authors proposed Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT), pairing positive samples with negative samples taken from the exact same elapsed timestamp, enabling a 2B model to finally beat the video-blind frontier by learning real visual cues.
stories.why_it_matters: A stark reminder for agent evaluation: always sanity-check multimodal benchmarks against trivial zero-shot heuristics like elapsed time before trusting leaderboards.
stories.reason: It demonstrates a severe evaluation shortcut where proactive assistant benchmarks inadvertently reward blind timing heuristics over true visual event verification.

item.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
item.summary: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. item.content:
Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
Abstract
Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.
Community
TL;DR: Existing benchmarks often reward timing-based shortcuts rather than genuine visual understanding. This paper introduces ECT, encouraging models to make decisions based on visual evidence instead of elapsed time. A simple yet effective approach toward more reliable proactive assistants.

item.title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
item.summary: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. item.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
item.summary: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.
